What Is a QR Code and How Does It Work?

A QR code is a square pattern of black and white modules that stores information, most often a web link, in a form a phone camera can read in a moment.

The short answer

QR stands for Quick Response. A QR code is a two-dimensional barcode: instead of a row of bars read left to right, it stores data in a grid of small squares, which lets it hold far more than an ordinary barcode. Pointing a phone camera at the pattern turns it back into text, such as a web address, a WiFi login, a phone number or a contact card.

The code itself is only a container. What happens next depends on what is inside: a link opens in the browser, a WiFi code offers to join a network, a contact code offers to save the person. Most current phones read QR codes with the ordinary camera app, without an extra app.

Where QR codes came from

QR codes were created in 1994 by Denso Wave, a Japanese company in the Toyota group, to track car parts on assembly lines. Ordinary barcodes held too little data and were slow to scan from an angle. The company chose to leave the specification open, which is a big reason QR codes spread so widely. The format is described in the international standard ISO/IEC 18004.

How a QR code works

A scanner does not look at a QR code like a picture. It finds specific patterns, reads the grid and applies error correction.

  1. The camera finds the three large squares in the corners. These finder patterns tell the scanner where the code is, how big it is and which way it is rotated.
  2. It reads the timing and alignment patterns that keep the grid straight, even when the code is on a curved or tilted surface.
  3. It reads format information that says which error correction level and mask were used.
  4. It reads the dark and light modules as bits and turns them back into data.
  5. It uses error correction to repair any parts that are dirty, damaged or hidden.

Parts of a QR code

Every QR code has the same building blocks.

PartWhat it does
Finder patterns (three corner squares)Show the scanner where the code is and how it is rotated
Alignment patternHelps correct distortion in larger codes
Timing patternsAlternating modules that define the grid
Format and version informationStore the error correction level and the code size
Data and error correction modulesHold your content and the extra data used for repair
Quiet zoneThe blank margin around the code, at least four modules wide in the specification

How much can a QR code hold?

Capacity depends on the size of the grid and the error correction level. QR codes come in 40 sizes called versions, from version 1 (21 by 21 modules) to version 40 (177 by 177 modules). At the largest size with the lowest error correction, a code can hold the following.

Type of dataMaximum characters (version 40, lowest error correction)
Numbers only7,089
Letters, numbers and a few symbols4,296
Any text (bytes)2,953

Error correction: why damaged codes still scan

QR codes carry extra data so a scanner can rebuild missing parts. There are four levels, and a higher level survives more damage but needs a denser, larger pattern.

  • L (low): repairs roughly 7% of the code.
  • M (medium): roughly 15%. A common default.
  • Q (quartile): roughly 25%.
  • H (high): roughly 30%. Used when a logo covers the center.

This is why a small logo in the middle of a QR code can still scan, and why it must stay small.

Types

What a QR code can contain

Web link

The most common use. Opens a page in the browser. Try the QR code generator.

WiFi login

Lets guests join a network without typing a password.

Contact card

A vCard that saves a name, number and email. See vCard QR codes.

Email, phone or SMS

Starts a message or call with details filled in.

Location

Opens a place in a maps app.

Calendar event

Adds an event to a calendar.

Payment details

Some regions use QR codes for payments, such as UPI in India or the GiroCode in Europe.

Plain text

Any text, such as a code or short note.

Static and dynamic QR codes

A static code has its content built into the pattern. A dynamic code contains a short link to a service that redirects to the real destination, which lets the destination change later and lets the service count scans. Read the full comparison in static vs dynamic QR codes.

How to use QR codes well

A QR code is only useful if people scan it and land somewhere worthwhile.

  • Say what it does. A short call to action such as "Scan for the menu" beats a bare code.
  • Print it large enough. Read the QR code size guide.
  • Keep contrast high. Dark code on a light background is safest.
  • Send people to a mobile-friendly page.
  • Test before you print, with the QR code tester and two real phones.
  • Be careful what you scan. See how to check a QR code is safe.
FAQ

QR Code Basics

QR stands for Quick Response. The name reflects the goal of the original design, which was to be read quickly.

Denso Wave, a Japanese company, created the QR code in 1994 to track car parts in factories.

Open your phone's camera app and point it at the code. Most current iPhones and Android phones show a link or an action. You can also use the online QR code scanner with an image or a webcam.

A static QR code never expires because its content is inside the pattern. It can stop being useful if the page it points to disappears. Dynamic codes can stop working if the service or subscription ends.

Scanning a code only reads its text. Risk comes from what you do next, such as opening a link or approving a payment. Check the destination first.

A traditional barcode stores a short number in a row of bars and is read by a scanner in a checkout. A QR code stores much more data in a square grid and is read by phone cameras. See the barcode generator for the other format.

Yes. Static QR codes are free to make on this site with no signup and no watermark.
